candidates.attacker_control: Whoever controls any configuration value that the application later reads as a String/List/array (e.g., an untrusted .properties/.xml/.yaml file loaded through FileBasedConfigurationBuilder, a config value assembled from environment/request data, a system/environment property used as a default). The attacker writes a value such as ${script:...} / ${url:...} / ${dns:...}; no application code change or api opt-in is required.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the lookups are not merely declared but actually installed by default: AbstractConfiguration.installDefaultInterpolator() (lines 452-456) installs ConfigurationInterpolator.getDefaultPrefixLookups(), and ConfigurationInterpolator.DEFAULT_PREFIX_LOOKUPS is populated from DefaultLookups.values() and Commons Text DefaultStringLookup.values() (lines 106-121). Checked that interpolation is applied to ordinary reads (AbstractConfiguration.getString(String,String) line 1351, getList lines 1428-1449) and that no deregistration/allow-list of script/dns/url occurs anywhere in the snapshot (searched for deregisterLookup/registerLookup usage). Also considered that config files are often trusted input, which lowers but does not remove the risk; the library itself advertises interpolation of configuration values.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the application's JVM when a script engine is available (script lookup); server-side request forgery and local file disclosure via url:file/http; DNS-based data exfiltration and internal host probing via the dns lookup. Values are interpolated by default with no allow-list or opt-in.
candidates.prerequisites: Application loads configuration data from a source that an attacker can influence (or stores attacker-influenced strings in a Configuration) and then reads that value through a normal getter, causing interpolation. For script execution, a JSR-223 script engine must be present on the classpath (e.g., Nashorn on JDK 8–14, or any other ScriptEngine); the dns/url lookups need no extra engine and enable DNS exfiltration and SSRF/file reads.
candidates.root_cause: ConfigurationInterpolator builds DEFAULT_PREFIX_LOOKUPS from DefaultLookups.values() plus DefaultStringLookup.values() from Commons Text, which include the 'script' (ScriptStringLookup), 'dns' (DnsStringLookup) and 'url' (UrlStringLookup) prefixes. AbstractConfiguration.installDefaultInterpolator() installs these defaults on every configuration instance, and AbstractConfiguration.interpolate()/getString()/getList() apply them to values read from configuration sources.
candidates.title: Dangerous default interpolation lookups (script/dns/url) enabled for every configuration value
candidates.trace: Config value read -> AbstractConfiguration.getString()/getList() -> AbstractConfiguration.interpolate(Object) -> ConfigurationInterpolator.interpolate() -> StringSubstitutor.replace() / resolveSingleVariable() -> ConfigurationInterpolator.resolve(var) (line 485-519) -> fetchLookupForPrefix('script'|'dns'|'url') -> lookups registered from DEFAULT_PREFIX_LOOKUPS (built at ConfigurationInterpolator lines 106-121 from DefaultLookups and Commons Text DefaultStringLookup) -> ScriptStringLookup executes the script, DnsStringLookup resolves the host, UrlStringLookup opens the URL.
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitability was not tested (no code execution). Whether the specific application treats the configuration source as attacker-controllable, and whether a JSR-223 engine is present on the runtime classpath (affects RCE vs. only dns/url impact), were not verifiable from the snapshot. The exact mapping of this snapshot to a particular benchmark ground-truth CVE could not be confirmed from source alone.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-470/94 (use of externally controlled data in code execution) / insecure default configuration permitting RCE, SSRF and information disclosure

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot of Apache Commons Configuration (318 model-visible files; all source under src/main/java plus site/changes/pom files; no tests are present in the snapshot). Deep inspection of: the interpolation package (ConfigurationInterpolator, DefaultLookups, ExprLookup, InterpolatorSpecification), AbstractConfiguration value-read/interpolation paths, beanutils (BeanHelper, DefaultBeanFactory, XMLBeanDeclaration), YAMLConfiguration/AbstractYAMLBasedConfiguration, XML configuration parsing setup (XMLConfiguration.createDocumentBuilder, XMLDocumentHelper, DefaultEntityResolver), and selected io classes (DefaultFileSystem, FileUtils, HomeDirectoryLocationStrategy, FileLocatorUtils beginning). Targeted literal searches for Runtime/ProcessBuilder/ObjectInputStream/ScriptEngine/Class.forName/new URL/openConnection/MessageDigest/InitialContext/XMLDecoder/setAccessible found no additional clearly injected sink. Large classes (PropertiesConfiguration, DataConfiguration, CombinedConfigurationBuilder, InMemoryNodeModel, ModelTransaction, DatabaseConfiguration, FileHandler) were only partially inspected; the P1 relation index was used as navigation only (syntactic candidates, no data-flow/runtime proof).
limitations: No tests, build, or runtime execution were available or performed; all conclusions are static-source based.

The snapshot is a development commit (pom 2.7-SNAPSHOT, changes through CONFIGURATION-779, ~early 2020); I could not confirm from source alone which upstream fix commit/benchmark ground truth this case corresponds to, so the mapping of the candidate to a specific CVE is uncertain.

Whether an attacker can actually influence the configuration source in the deploying application, and whether a JSR-223 script engine is present at runtime (conditioning RCE versus SSRF/DNS impact), is deployment-dependent and unverified.
Several large files were reviewed only partially; other latent issues (e.g., include-path handling in PropertiesConfiguration, node-model and reloading code) were not exhaustively traced.
No external data, CVE databases, patches, or previous outputs were consulted per the review constraints.

rejected_leads.lead: BeanHelper/DefaultBeanFactory/XMLBeanDeclaration instantiate arbitrary classes named by the 'config-class' attribute from configuration (src/main/java/org/apache/commons/configuration2/beanutils/BeanHelper.java lines 538-566, DefaultBeanFactory.java lines 140-148)
rejected_leads.reason: This is documented, intended library behavior (bean creation from configuration is a feature used by CombinedConfigurationBuilder for providers/lookups); exploitation requires the application to feed an untrusted bean declaration into BeanHelper. I found no local validation/allow-list, but could not verify that a benchmark-relevant fix/CVE targets this file, so it remains an unconfirmed lead rather than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: YAMLConfiguration.read() uses SnakeYAML new Yaml()/yaml.load() default constructor, which can instantiate arbitrary tags (src/main/java/org/apache/commons/configuration2/YAMLConfiguration.java lines 64-91, 116-143)
rejected_leads.reason: Genuine unsafe default (arbitrary object instantiation via YAML tags), but the same pattern exists throughout this era of the library and the snapshot contains LoaderOptions overloads only as caller-provided options with no default hardening. Impact is real but the library's YAML readers are documented as parsing configuration data, and I could not confirm this is the case's ground-truth issue.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLConfiguration/DefaultEntityResolver allow DTD/external entity resolution by default (DefaultEntityResolver.java lines 84-114 returns null for unregistered entities; XMLConfiguration.createDocumentBuilder() lines 838-873 sets no secure-processing features)
rejected_leads.reason: Potential XXE when parsing untrusted XML configuration, but it depends on the parser's default entity handling and on an attacker feeding XML config; no explicit check disabling DTDs exists, yet this is a standard JAXP-default situation and was not confirmed as the intended finding.

rejected_leads.lead: DatabaseConfiguration builds SQL statements using configuration-supplied table/column/key names (DatabaseConfiguration.java around lines 354, 370-404, 461-493, 536-581, 849)
rejected_leads.reason: SQL text is assembled from values that in common usage come from the application's own configuration, not from a remote attacker; no evidence of untrusted-input flow was established, so it was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultFileSystem.getOutputStream(URL) performs an HTTP PUT / arbitrary URL write when a configuration is saved to a non-file URL (DefaultFileSystem.java lines 58-95)
rejected_leads.reason: Requires the application to save to an attacker-chosen URL, which is a misuse of the save API rather than a demonstrated attacker-controlled flow; rejected as weaker than the selected candidate.

summary: Apache Commons Configuration 2.7-SNAPSHOT snapshot (pom version 2.7-SNAPSHOT, changes through CONFIGURATION-779). The strongest source-evidenced issue is the default interpolation lookup set: every AbstractConfiguration installs ConfigurationInterpolator.DEFAULT_PREFIX_LOOKUPS, which (in this snapshot) contains the Commons Text lookups "script", "dns" and "url" in addition to the library's own DefaultLookups entries. Because interpolation runs on ordinary value reads, any configuration string containing ${script:...}, ${dns:...} or ${url:...} is evaluated with no opt-in, giving attacker-controlled config values access to script-engine execution (RCE where a JSR-223 engine such as Nashorn is available), DNS lookups (exfiltration) and URL fetches (SSRF/local file reads). This matches the well-known CVE-2022-33980 issue for versions 2.4–2.7. No source-level mitigation (removal/allow-listing of these default lookups) exists in this snapshot. Other code smells (config-class bean instantiation, unsafe SnakeYAML default, XML entity resolution) are noted as rejected/unconfirmed leads because they are either documented-by-design or require assumptions I could not verify from this snapshot.
